```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 8,
  fig.align = "center",
  fig.retina = 2,
  out.width = "100%"

```

## 1. The statistical problem: subgroup treatment effects and interactions

Consider a meta-analysis in which clinical trials report treatment
effects separately for two patient subgroups, such as patients with
lower or higher baseline disability. We may be interested both in the
average treatment effect within each subgroup and in whether the
treatment effect differs between subgroups, commonly referred to as a
treatment-by-subgroup interaction.

Several approaches are available for estimating these quantities from
subgroup-level aggregate data. Two commonly used approaches are the
difference of averages (DA) and the average difference (AD). Although
both use the same reported subgroup estimates, they need not yield the
same interaction estimate.

The running example is `edss`, from a systematic review of
immunotherapies for relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (Heesen,
Röver, Salem et al. 2024). The outcome is the effect on the relapse
rate. An incidence-rate ratio below 1 means a lower relapse rate on
treatment than on control. The subgroups are lower and higher baseline
EDSS (Expanded Disability Status Scale). The dataset records those two
labels and does not store the numeric EDSS cut. The active treatment
differs across comparisons. The analysis follows the published review
and combines the reported effects.

CONFIRM contributes two active treatments, BG-12 and copaxone, that
share a control group. The code gives those rows separate comparison
labels, CONFIRM-B and CONFIRM-C, so that later calls, which group by
`trial` and `subgroup`, do not pool them. The comparisons are then
treated as separate analysis units. Dependence from the shared control
is not modeled.

```{r edss-define}
library(interact)

edss_ex <- edss
edss_ex$trial <- as.character(edss_ex$trial)
confirm <- edss_ex$trial == "CONFIRM"
edss_ex$trial[confirm & edss_ex$treatment == "BG-12"] <- "CONFIRM-B"
edss_ex$trial[confirm & edss_ex$treatment == "copaxone"] <- "CONFIRM-C"

edss_ex[edss_ex$trial == "DEFINE", c("trial", "subgroup", "n", "treatment", "yi", "vi")]
```

The prepared data are in long format: each row contains one
subgroup-specific treatment-effect estimate and its sampling variance,
so a comparison reporting both EDSS subgroups contributes two rows.
DEFINE shows the layout: `n` is the sample size, `yi` the log
incidence-rate ratio, and `vi` its sampling variance.

**Difference of averages.** Pool the lower-EDSS estimates, pool the
higher-EDSS estimates, and subtract. On the log scale

$$
\gamma_{\mathrm{DA}} = \mu_{\mathrm{Higher}} - \mu_{\mathrm{Lower}}.
$$

Exponentiating gives the ratio of the two pooled incidence-rate
ratios. The lower-EDSS subgroup is the reference, so the interaction
compares the higher-EDSS subgroup with the lower-EDSS subgroup.

**Average difference.** Within each comparison, form

$$
g_j = y_{\mathrm{Higher},j} - y_{\mathrm{Lower},j}
$$

and meta-analyse the contrasts $g_j$. The pooled contrast is the
interaction. AD does not return a treatment effect for either EDSS
subgroup on its own. That pooled contrast and the DA interaction do
not in general agree, because the two subgroup meta-analyses need not
use the same weights. When the aim is the treatment-by-subgroup
interaction, an analysis based on the within-comparison contrasts,
such as AD, is preferable to relying on DA alone.

**Shared weights.** Same weighting across different analyses (SWADA)
applies a common set of study weights when pooling the treatment
effects in the lower- and higher-EDSS subgroups (Panaro, Röver & Friede
2026a). With the default weights taken from AD, the difference between
these two pooled subgroup effects equals the pooled within-comparison
interaction. SWADA therefore provides two subgroup effect estimates
and an interaction estimate that agree by construction. When one
subgroup contributes nearly all the precision, the common weights can
be dominated by that subgroup. That agreement does not guarantee that
both subgroup effects are well informed. In `interact`, SWADA is
currently implemented for frequentist inference only; its
common-weighting construction is an estimation procedure rather than a
separately specified Bayesian model.

`interact` fits these calculations by restricted maximum likelihood.
`reference = "Lower"` sets the direction of the interaction. The
table reports each interaction as an incidence-rate ratio with its
95% confidence interval.

```{r interactions}
fit_da <- da(edss_ex, reference = "Lower", engine = "metafor")
fit_ad <- ad(edss_ex, reference = "Lower", engine = "metafor")
fit_sw <- swada(edss_ex, reference = "Lower", engine = "metafor")
ix <- t(sapply(list(DA = fit_da, AD = fit_ad, SWADA = fit_sw), function(fit) {
  s <- tidy(interactions(fit, exponentiate = TRUE))
  c(estimate = s$estimate, conf.low = s$conf.low, conf.high = s$conf.high)
}))
knitr::kable(ix, digits = 2)
```

In this example the three point estimates agree and the intervals do
not. The DA interval includes 1. The AD and SWADA intervals exclude 1.
DA pools each subgroup separately, so the two meta-analyses can use
different weights and each has its own heterogeneity. AD
meta-analyses the within-comparison contrasts and uses the
heterogeneity of those contrasts. Unequal weights, or those separate
variance calculations, can move the estimate or the interval.
Reporting both subgroups in every comparison does not by itself make
the results agree. `compare_weights()` tabulates the study shares.
SWADA uses the AD weights, which is why those two interactions agree.

SWADA aligns the interaction with AD by imposing those shared weights.
Contribution-adjusted meta-analysis (CAMS) takes a further step: it
specifies a statistical model that links the subgroup treatment
effects and their interaction through the information fractions.
Related models include the bivariate mixed model of van Houwelingen,
Arends and Stijnen (2002) and the within-trial framework of Godolphin
et al. (2023).

## 2. Information fractions and the CAMS model

Within a comparison, the lower- and higher-EDSS estimates are not
equally precise. The precision of an estimate is the reciprocal of its
sampling variance. CAMS records the higher-EDSS subgroup's share of
that precision, and uses the share to link the subgroup treatment
effects with their interaction. With the lower-EDSS subgroup as the
reference, this information fraction is the higher-EDSS subgroup's
share. It is not the proportion of patients in the higher-EDSS group:
for an incidence-rate ratio, the sampling variance depends on the
number of events as well as on the sample size.

For comparison $j$, let $\sigma_{Aj}^2$ and $\sigma_{Bj}^2$ denote the
sampling variances of the lower- and higher-EDSS estimates. These are
the reported values `vi`, treated as known. The higher-EDSS subgroup's
information fraction is

$$
\pi_j =
\frac{1/\sigma_{Bj}^2}{1/\sigma_{Aj}^2 + 1/\sigma_{Bj}^2}.
$$

The numerator is the higher-EDSS subgroup's precision and the
denominator is the total, so $0 < \pi_j < 1$. `ifrac()` calculates
these shares from the reported sampling variances. In DEFINE the
patient share and the information fraction are close. In AFFIRM the
higher-EDSS subgroup is a smaller share of the patients than of the
precision.

```{r edss-ifrac, echo = FALSE}
edss_if <- ifrac(edss_ex, reference = "Lower")
higher <- edss_if[edss_if$subgroup == "Higher", c("trial", "n", "ifrac_Higher")]
lower_n <- edss_if[edss_if$subgroup == "Lower", c("trial", "n")]
pair <- merge(lower_n, higher, by = "trial", suffixes = c("_lower", "_higher"))
shown <- pair[match(c("DEFINE", "AFFIRM"), pair$trial), ]
shown$patient_share <- shown$n_higher / (shown$n_lower + shown$n_higher)
knitr::kable(
  shown[, c("trial", "patient_share", "ifrac_Higher")],
  digits = 3
)
```

Across comparisons the higher-EDSS fractions run from about
`r format(round(min(pair$ifrac_Higher), 2), nsmall = 2)` to about
`r format(round(max(pair$ifrac_Higher), 2), nsmall = 2)`.

The within-comparison contrast is the higher-EDSS estimate minus the
lower-EDSS estimate,

$$
g_j = y_{Bj} - y_{Aj},
$$

the treatment-by-subgroup contrast on the log scale. The combined
estimate weights each subgroup by its precision,

$$
m_j = (1 - \pi_j)\, y_{Aj} + \pi_j\, y_{Bj}.
$$

The more precise subgroup receives the greater weight. The contrast
variance is the sum of the two subgroup variances, and the combined
estimate has the smaller variance. At this information fraction the
sampling covariance of $g_j$ and $m_j$ is zero.

### The model

CAMS is a random-effects model for $g_j$ and $m_j$ (Panaro, Röver &
Friede 2025). Separating the likelihood uses three assumptions.

First, the sampling errors of the two subgroup estimates are
independent conditional on the underlying comparison-specific treatment
effects $\mu_{Aj}$ and $\mu_{Bj}$. The sampling distributions are
normal, and the current implementation assumes that the conditional
sampling covariance is zero:

$$
y_{Aj} \mid \mu_{Aj} \sim \mathrm{Normal}(\mu_{Aj}, \sigma_{Aj}^2), \qquad
y_{Bj} \mid \mu_{Bj} \sim \mathrm{Normal}(\mu_{Bj}, \sigma_{Bj}^2).
$$

Then

$$
\mathrm{Var}(g_j) = \sigma_{Aj}^2 + \sigma_{Bj}^2, \qquad
\mathrm{Var}(m_j) = \left(\frac{1}{\sigma_{Aj}^2} +
\frac{1}{\sigma_{Bj}^2}\right)^{-1},
$$

and $\mathrm{Cov}(g_j, m_j) = 0$, so the sampling distribution of
$(g_j, m_j)$ factors into two univariate distributions. This concerns
the two estimates inside one comparison. It does not make the observed
subgroup estimates marginally independent once the random effects are
integrated out, and dependence between comparisons, including
CONFIRM-B and CONFIRM-C, remains unmodeled. Each $\pi_j$ is computed
from the variances before fitting and is a known covariate.

Second, the random effect in the combined-effect model and the random
effect in the interaction model are independent. This is a separate
assumption. Zero sampling covariance does not imply it, and zero
sampling covariance alone does not factor the hierarchical likelihood.

Under these assumptions, the likelihood separates into an interaction
meta-analysis and a combined-effect meta-regression. The contrasts
follow

$$
g_j = \gamma + \delta_j + e_j, \qquad
\delta_j \sim \mathrm{Normal}(0, \tau_g^2),
$$

where $e_j$ is the sampling error of $g_j$. The parameter $\gamma$ is
the mean interaction, and $\tau_g$ is its heterogeneity. The combined
estimates follow

$$
m_j = \alpha + \theta \pi_j + u_j + \varepsilon_j, \qquad
u_j \sim \mathrm{Normal}(0, \tau_m^2),
$$

where $\varepsilon_j$ is the sampling error of $m_j$, and the $u_j$ are
independent of the $\delta_j$. The fitted combined mean at information
fraction $\pi$ is $M(\pi) = \alpha + \theta \pi$. The intercept $\alpha$
is the mean combined effect at $\pi = 0$, and $\theta$ is its change as
the higher-EDSS subgroup's share of the precision increases.
$\tau_m$ is the heterogeneity about that line. Here $m_j$ is the
observed combined effect for comparison $j$; $M(\pi)$ is the
population-level mean.

The subgroup means follow from $M(\pi)$ and the common interaction:

$$
\mu_A(\pi) = M(\pi) - \pi \gamma, \qquad
\mu_B(\pi) = M(\pi) + (1 - \pi)\, \gamma.
$$

Their difference remains $\gamma$ at every information fraction. Both
subgroup means have slope $\theta - \gamma$, while $M(\pi)$ has slope
$\theta$. The combined mean is the precision-weighted average of the
subgroup means at the same $\pi$,

$$
M(\pi) = (1 - \pi)\, \mu_A(\pi) + \pi\, \mu_B(\pi),
$$

not the effect in a population of which a fraction $\pi$ has higher
baseline EDSS. By allowing the mean subgroup effects to depend on the
information fraction while keeping their difference constant, CAMS
models an ecological association with that precision share that could
otherwise be mistaken for a difference in treatment response.

Overall subgroup effects are quoted at a reporting information
fraction, a weighted average of the trial-specific values $\pi_j$.
`cams()` can fit this model by Bayesian or frequentist methods. The
fit that follows is Bayesian.

## 3. A first analysis using interact

`cams()` estimates these parameters from the prepared `edss`
comparisons. It computes the information fractions internally from the
subgroup sampling variances, so those values do not need to be passed
separately. The call below is Bayesian. The priors on the heterogeneity
standard deviations are set explicitly: a half-normal distribution with
scale 0.5 for $\tau_m$, the combined-effect heterogeneity, and scale
0.1 for $\tau_g$, the interaction heterogeneity.

```{r fit-edss}
fit_edss <- cams(
  edss_ex,
  reference = "Lower",
  tau.prior = function(tau) bayesmeta::dhalfnormal(tau, scale = 0.5),
  tau.interaction.prior = function(tau) bayesmeta::dhalfnormal(tau, scale = 0.1)
)
```

These are not the package defaults. The half-normal scales follow
Panaro, Röver & Friede (2026b). A half-normal prior is supported
only on non-negative values, and a larger scale gives more prior
weight to large heterogeneity. The scale 0.1 on $\tau_g$ is tighter
than the scale 0.5 on $\tau_m$. By default, `cams()` uses improper
uniform priors for the two heterogeneity standard deviations. The
coefficients $\alpha$ and $\theta$ in the combined-effect model and the
interaction parameter $\gamma$ have independent normal priors with mean
0 and standard deviation 10.

`reference = "Lower"` keeps the direction used above, so $\gamma$
compares the higher-EDSS subgroup with the lower-EDSS subgroup. The
fit is on the log incidence-rate-ratio scale. `exponentiate = TRUE`
reports incidence-rate ratios. A ratio below 1 means a lower relapse
rate on treatment than on control.

The table gives the interaction $\gamma$, the subgroup means
$\mu_A(\pi)$ and $\mu_B(\pi)$, and the combined mean $M(\pi)$. The
subgroup and combined means are evaluated at one reporting information
fraction, the default interaction-weighted average of the
trial-specific values $\pi_j$, rather than at each comparison's own
$\pi_j$. `Overall` is the mean effect, with a credible interval.
`Prediction` is the underlying effect in a new comparison that is
exchangeable with the comparisons under the fitted random-effects
model. It includes heterogeneity, so it is wider, and it does not
account for dependence or other structure that the model leaves out.

```{r edss-results, echo = FALSE}
ix <- tidy(interactions(fit_edss, exponentiate = TRUE))
sg <- tidy(subgroups(fit_edss, exponentiate = TRUE))
cb <- tidy(combined(fit_edss, exponentiate = TRUE))
part <- function(quantity, d) {
  data.frame(
    quantity = quantity,
    type = d$type,
    estimate = d$estimate,
    conf.low = d$conf.low,
    conf.high = d$conf.high
  )
}
knitr::kable(
  rbind(
    part("Interaction", ix),
    part(paste(sg$subgroup, "subgroup"), sg),
    part("Combined", cb)
  ),
  digits = 2
)
```

The interaction credible interval lies above 1, so the higher-EDSS
incidence-rate ratio is estimated to be larger than the lower-EDSS
ratio. Both pooled subgroup ratios are below 1: the mean relapse rate
is estimated to be lower on treatment in each EDSS subgroup, and the
higher-EDSS ratio is closer to 1. The interaction above 1 means a
smaller benefit in the higher-EDSS subgroup, not an absence of
benefit. The prediction intervals are wider; for the subgroups and the
combined effect they extend above 1. The combined credible interval
excludes 1. Its prediction interval is the uncertainty for a new
exchangeable comparison, not a second estimate of the mean.

## 4. Interpreting pooled subgroup effects and information fractions

The reporting value used above is a weighted average of the
trial-specific fractions $\pi_j$. Comparisons that are estimated more
precisely receive more weight. That average is still a summary of
precision. It is not the proportion of patients with higher baseline
EDSS.

Write $\omega(\tau)$ for the reporting information fraction. With
weights $w_j(\tau)$ that depend on a heterogeneity standard deviation
$\tau$,

$$
\omega(\tau) =
\frac{\sum_j \pi_j w_j(\tau)}{\sum_j w_j(\tau)}.
$$

The weights are the usual random-effects weights, one over heterogeneity
variance plus sampling variance. The default, `ifrac = "interaction"`,
takes those weights from the meta-analysis of the contrasts $g_j$, so
$\tau$ is $\tau_g$. The alternative, `ifrac = "overall"`, takes them
from the meta-regression of the combined estimates $m_j$, so $\tau$ is
$\tau_m$. Heterogeneity is uncertain in this Bayesian model, so
$\omega(\tau)$ has a posterior distribution.

```{r edss-omega}
ifrac(fit_edss)
ifrac(fit_edss, ifrac = "overall")
```

The two summaries are close, and both lie inside the range of the
trial-specific fractions. Every comparison's higher-EDSS share is well
below one half, so 0.5 is outside the observed range. The interaction
$\gamma$ does not depend on $\pi$. Evaluating the subgroup and combined
means at another fraction inside that range would move those means.
It would not move the interaction.

`plot_contribution()` draws the mean functions against the information
fraction. The points are the reported subgroup estimates at each
comparison's own $\pi_j$. With `exponentiate = TRUE` the curves are
incidence-rate ratios. On that scale the ratio of the two subgroup
means is constant, and the combined-effect curve lies between them.
These curves are fitted estimates. A visible change with the
information fraction does not by itself show that the ecological slope
$\theta - \gamma$ differs from zero. The shaded bands describe
uncertainty in the fitted means at each information fraction.

```{r edss-contribution, fig.height = 5}
plot_contribution(fit_edss, exponentiate = TRUE)
```

## 5. Forest plots and trial-specific shrinkage estimates

The contribution plot shows the fitted mean functions. `forestplot()`
shows the same model one comparison at a time. `exponentiate = TRUE`
shows incidence-rate ratios, and the horizontal axis is logarithmic.
Values below 1 are lower relapse rates on treatment. The figure has
one panel for each EDSS subgroup. The note under the axis reports the
reporting information fraction and the two heterogeneity standard
deviations.

```{r edss-forest, fig.height = 8}
forestplot(
  fit_edss,
  exponentiate = TRUE,
  favours = c("Lower relapse rate", "Higher relapse rate")
)
```

The black squares are the published subgroup estimates, with intervals
from the reported sampling variances. The IF column is the information
contributed by that subgroup within the comparison: $\pi_j$ for the
higher-EDSS subgroup and $1 - \pi_j$ for the lower-EDSS subgroup. Those
fractions sum to one. They are separate from the reporting fraction in
the note under the axis.

The grey diamonds are subgroup-specific shrinkage estimates. For each
comparison, the combined effect is shrunk toward the combined-effect
mean and the interaction is shrunk toward $\gamma$; the subgroup
effects are then recovered at that comparison's own information
fraction. The pooled diamond is the mean subgroup effect at the
reporting information fraction, the same summary as the subgroup rows
above. The grey diamond belongs to one comparison. The pooled diamond
does not. The prediction row is the prediction interval from the
results table. The article on
[trial-specific effects and shrinkage](trial-specific-effects-and-shrinkage.html)
follows one comparison through this re-expression.

## 6. Frequentist and Bayesian inference

A frequentist fit estimates the same CAMS model as the Bayesian fit
already obtained. Both target the interaction $\gamma$, the subgroup
means, and the reporting information fraction. They differ in how the
parameters are estimated and in how uncertainty is represented. The
Bayesian fit uses the half-normal priors set above. The frequentist
fit uses restricted maximum likelihood (REML).

```{r edss-reml}
fit_edss_reml <- cams(
  edss_ex,
  reference = "Lower",
  engine = "metafor",
  method = "REML"
)
```

In the Bayesian analysis the parameters have a posterior distribution.
A posterior median is the central estimate, and a credible interval is
a range that contains the parameter with the stated posterior
probability under the model. Uncertainty in the heterogeneity standard
deviations is part of that posterior, so it is carried into the
interaction, the subgroup means, and the reporting fraction.

REML instead returns a point estimate of each parameter, including a
point estimate of each heterogeneity standard deviation. Those
estimated heterogeneity values are then used in the weights and in the
interval calculations. A confidence interval is a range from a
procedure that covers the parameter at the stated rate across repeated
samples. The Bayesian table marks intervals through the posterior. The
frequentist tables below mark them as Wald confidence intervals.

$\tau_m$ is the combined-effect heterogeneity and $\tau_g$ is the
interaction heterogeneity. `plot_heterogeneity()` draws their marginal
posteriors from `fit_edss`. The panels share vertical limits, so the
height of one curve can be compared with the height of the other.
Each panel keeps its own horizontal range. The interaction posterior
lies on a shorter interval, and a common range out to the
combined-effect tail would compress it.

```{r edss-het, fig.height = 4}
plot_heterogeneity(fit_edss)
```

The left panel is $\tau_m$, labelled $\tau$. The right panel is
$\tau_g$, labelled $\tau_\gamma$. The darker shading is a 95% credible
interval, and the line inside it is the posterior median. In this fit
the interaction posterior is concentrated near zero, with its median
near 0.07. The combined-effect posterior has median near 0.28. A
taller curve is a more concentrated posterior, not a larger
heterogeneity, and the figure is not a comparison of the mean
treatment effects. The prior scale is 0.1 for $\tau_g$ and 0.5 for
$\tau_m$, and that tighter interaction prior contributes to the
concentration.

The trial-specific information fractions are computed from the reported
sampling variances before either fit, so they do not depend on the
inferential approach. The reporting fraction is a heterogeneity-weighted
average of those $\pi_j$. It is a posterior distribution in the
Bayesian fit and a single number, at the estimated heterogeneity, in
the REML fit. The comparison below uses the mean effects on the
incidence-rate-ratio scale.

```{r edss-reml-effects}
interactions(fit_edss_reml, type = "Overall", exponentiate = TRUE)
subgroups(fit_edss_reml, type = "Overall", exponentiate = TRUE)
```

The REML interaction agrees with the AD interaction, because both are
random-effects meta-analyses of the same contrasts. The REML subgroup
estimates agree with the Bayesian table at two decimals. The subgroup
intervals are somewhat wider in the Bayesian fit. The approaches differ
in how they account for heterogeneity uncertainty, and the Bayesian
analysis additionally depends on the specified priors.

Maximum likelihood is the other frequentist option, selected with
`method = "ML"`. It estimates heterogeneity by maximum likelihood
rather than by REML. No maximum-likelihood fit is shown here.

## 7. Trials reporting only one subgroup

Every comparison in the EDSS example reported both subgroups. Some
trials do not.

The `steroids` data come from the WHO REACT prospective meta-analysis
of systemic corticosteroids in critically ill patients with COVID-19
(Sterne, Murthy et al. 2020). The outcome is mortality. Each comparison
is an odds ratio for corticosteroids versus control, and an odds ratio
below 1 means lower odds of death on corticosteroids. The subgroups are
invasively ventilated patients (IV) and patients who received
non-invasive support (NIV).

Four trials report both subgroups. CoDEX, DEXA-COVID 19, and RECOVERY
report only IV patients. Each unreported NIV cell is stored as a row
with `n = 0`. Here, `n = 0` indicates that the subgroup was not
reported; it is different from a reported subgroup with zero observed
events. Those rows are not observed outcomes.

A trial that reports only IV patients informs the IV treatment effect.
It does not contain both subgroup estimates, so it does not directly
identify the within-trial interaction
\(g_j = y_{\mathrm{IV},j} - y_{\mathrm{NIV},j}\).

Odds ratios are calculated from the reported counts after the empty
rows are removed. `ifrac()` then inserts a placeholder for each
unreported NIV cell: a log odds ratio of 0 with sampling variance
\(100^2\). The placeholder is a computational device. It makes the
trial-by-subgroup table complete. It is not an observed treatment
effect, and it is not an imputation of the unreported NIV effect. The
value 0 is arbitrary. Because the variance is finite, the cell's
contribution is negligible rather than exactly zero. Were that variance
infinite, the IV information fraction would be 1 and the interaction
contrast would have infinite variance. Filling the table is data
preparation. The statistical model is unchanged.

`reference = "NIV"` makes $\pi_j$ the IV share of the precision. With
the placeholder, that share is close to 1. An IV-only trial contributes
its IV treatment effect to the combined-effect analysis and receives
negligible weight in the interaction. The interaction is identified by
the four complete trials: CAPE COVID, COVID STEROID, REMAP-CAP, and
Steroids-SARI.

```{r steroids-fit}
steroids_obs <- steroids[steroids$n > 0, ]
steroids_es <- escalc(
  measure = "OR",
  ai = treat.events,
  bi = treat.total - treat.events,
  ci = cont.events,
  di = cont.total - cont.events,
  data = steroids_obs
)
des <- ifrac(steroids_es, reference = "NIV")
fit_da_st <- da(des, reference = "NIV", engine = "metafor")
fit_ad_st <- ad(des, reference = "NIV", engine = "metafor")
fit_st <- cams(
  des,
  reference = "NIV",
  engine = "metafor",
  method = "REML"
)
```

The table compares the IV-versus-NIV interaction odds ratios.

```{r steroids-interactions, echo = FALSE}
ix <- t(sapply(list(DA = fit_da_st, AD = fit_ad_st, CAMS = fit_st), function(fit) {
  s <- tidy(interactions(fit, type = "Overall", exponentiate = TRUE))
  c(estimate = s$estimate, conf.low = s$conf.low, conf.high = s$conf.high)
}))
knitr::kable(ix, digits = 2)
```

AD and CAMS agree with each other. The DA interval includes 1; the AD
and CAMS intervals do not. The IV-only trials move the DA estimate for
the IV subgroup. They do not identify \(g_j\).

Interaction weights give the IV-only trials negligible weight, so the
interaction-weighted reporting fraction summarizes the complete trials.
Combined weights use their IV precision, and RECOVERY, the largest IV
comparison, pulls that fraction toward 1. Each value is evaluated at
the estimated heterogeneity. Neither fraction is a population
proportion.

```{r steroids-fractions, echo = FALSE}
ifrac(fit_st, ifrac = "interaction")
ifrac(fit_st, ifrac = "overall")
sg_at <- function(which) {
  s <- tidy(subgroups(
    fit_st, type = "Overall", exponentiate = TRUE, ifrac = which
  ))
  data.frame(
    reporting = which,
    subgroup = s$subgroup,
    estimate = s$estimate,
    conf.low = s$conf.low,
    conf.high = s$conf.high
  )
}
knitr::kable(
  rbind(sg_at("interaction"), sg_at("overall")),
  digits = 2
)
```

The subgroup odds ratios change between the two reporting fractions.
The interaction does not. The different subgroup estimates are the same
fitted functions evaluated at different information fractions, not a
refit of the model.

`forestplot()` draws this fit at the interaction-weighted reporting
fraction. An odds ratio below 1 is lower mortality on corticosteroids.

```{r steroids-forest, fig.height = 8}
forestplot(
  fit_st,
  exponentiate = TRUE,
  favours = c("Lower mortality", "Higher mortality")
)
```

For CoDEX, DEXA-COVID 19, and RECOVERY, the IV information fractions
are at or extremely close to 100%, and the NIV rows have no published
estimate. A grey diamond for a subgroup the trial did not report is a
model-based trial-specific estimate, not an observed subgroup effect.
The wide COVID STEROID interval is the sampling interval of a small
observed comparison. In this fit both heterogeneity standard
deviations, $\tau_m$ and $\tau_g$, are estimated as zero. These are
boundary estimates. They do not establish the absence of true
heterogeneity. Because the estimates are zero, the pooled confidence
intervals and the prediction intervals coincide.

## 8. Additional datasets and functionality

The examples above use `edss` and `steroids`. The package also includes
`age`, `il6`, `respire_age`, and `respire_sex`. All six are
subgroup-level aggregate data in long format. The model is fitted on
the log scale stored in `yi`. For log-ratio effect measures, such as
log odds ratios, log incidence-rate ratios, and log hazard ratios,
`exponentiate = TRUE` reports the corresponding ratio. Estimates
expressed as mean differences remain on the difference scale and
should not ordinarily be exponentiated.

| Dataset | Patients and comparison | Subgroups | Effect measure |
|---|---|---|---|
| `age` | Immunotherapies for relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis; relapse | Younger, Older | Log incidence-rate ratio |
| `edss` | The same review; relapse | Lower, Higher baseline EDSS | Log incidence-rate ratio |
| `steroids` | Systemic corticosteroids in critically ill COVID-19; mortality | IV, NIV | Log odds ratio, from event counts |
| `il6` | IL-6 antagonists in patients hospitalized for COVID-19; mortality | Corticosteroids `yes`, `no` | Log odds ratio, from event counts |
| `respire_age` | Ciprofloxacin dry-powder inhalation in non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis; time to first exacerbation | `<65`, `>=65` | Log hazard ratio |
| `respire_sex` | The same trials and endpoint | Female, Male | Log hazard ratio |

`age` and `edss` come from Heesen, Röver, Salem et al. (2024). In the
raw `edss` table, CONFIRM contributes two treatments under one trial
identifier; the EDSS example separates those rows, and dependence from
the shared control is not modeled. `steroids` comes from Sterne, Murthy
et al. (2020), and `il6` from Sterne, Murthy et al. (2021). Like
`steroids`, some `il6` trials report only one subgroup; empty rows are
stored with `n = 0`. `respire_age` and `respire_sex` come from the
RESPIRE 1 and RESPIRE 2 trials (De Soyza et al. 2018; Aksamit et al.
2018). Both subgroups are reported in each trial. The stored `yi` and
`vi` are log hazard ratios and their variances. The published intervals
used to derive them are not all 95% intervals.
